page.metaDescription: How to evaluate website monitoring tools: feature checklists, pricing models, common limitations, and which tool fits which use case.
page.h1: Website monitoring tools: how to compare them
page.subtitle: Feature checklists, pricing-model tradeoffs, and honest limits across the website-monitoring tool category.
page.intro: The website-monitoring category has dozens of tools that look superficially similar — paste a URL, get alerts. The real differences show up after you've been using a tool for a month. This guide covers what to look for when evaluating, what the pricing models actually mean for your usage pattern, and where each major tool category fits.

sections.title: Categories of website monitoring tools
sections.body: Uptime-only monitors (Pingdom, UptimeRobot, StatusCake) focus on HTTP health checks. Change-detection tools (Visualping, Distill, Wachete) catch any visual or text change on a page. AI-enabled tools (WebMonitor.fyi and a handful of others) use language models for criteria interpretation. Full-stack synthetic monitoring (Datadog, New Relic) is a much heavier solution with APM integration. Most teams need one from this list; some combine two.

sections.title: Pricing models and what they actually mean
sections.body: Per-monitor pricing favors users with stable monitor counts. Per-check pricing favors infrequent checking. Per-account flat pricing favors heavy users with many monitors. A tool that's "cheap" at 10 monitors can be expensive at 200; the inverse is also true. Calculate the cost based on your actual usage — number of monitors × check frequency × month — before signing up.

sections.title: Feature checklist
sections.body: Check intervals available (minimum and maximum). Delivery channels (email is universal; SMS, webhook, Slack, PagerDuty vary). Criteria flexibility (fixed selectors vs natural language vs regex). Multi-region check support. Authentication support for gated pages (most tools: no). Bulk monitor management for 50+ monitors. Export and reporting. Retention of historical alert data. Each of these is non-obvious until you need it.

sections.title: Common limitations across the category
sections.body: Login-gated pages are hard for every tool; check whether yours handles them. Pages with aggressive anti-bot measures (Cloudflare's strictest tier, PerimeterX-protected sites) get blocked by most tools. JavaScript-heavy pages where content loads after the initial response need a browser-rendering mode that not all tools offer. Real-time tick data (financial feeds, betting odds) is a separate category — monitoring tools aren't the right fit.

sections.title: How to evaluate before committing
sections.body: Set up monitors on 5 representative pages you care about. Let them run for a week. Check: did real changes fire alerts? Did cosmetic changes fire false alerts? Was the delivery latency acceptable? Was the dashboard pleasant to use at scale? A one-week trial covers more than a feature comparison spreadsheet.
